parts.move: define angular velocity and state its unit
parts.prompt: Define angular velocity and state its SI unit.
scheme: Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement
Measured in radians per second (rad s⁻¹)
parts.answer: Angular velocity is the rate of change of angle swept out per unit time, measured in radians per second (rad s⁻¹).

parts.move: state the relation between linear and angular speed
parts.prompt: State the equation relating the linear speed v of a point on a rotating body to its angular velocity ω and radius r.
scheme: v = ωr
The linear speed grows in direct proportion to both ω and the radius
parts.answer: v = ωr: a point's linear speed is its angular velocity multiplied by its distance from the rotation axis.

parts.move: explain why riders at different radii share angular velocity but not linear speed
parts.prompt: Two children sit on a rotating roundabout, one near the centre and one at the edge. Explain why they have the same angular velocity but different linear speeds.
scheme: Both sweep out the same angle per second, so ω is equal
v = ωr, and the edge child has the larger r
The edge child therefore moves faster in m s⁻¹ despite the same rad s⁻¹
parts.answer: Sitting on the same rigid roundabout, both children turn through the same angle every second — same ω. But v = ωr, so the child at the larger radius has the proportionally larger linear speed.

parts.move: convert a rotation rate in rev min⁻¹ to angular velocity and edge speed
parts.prompt: A ceiling fan spins at 210 rev min⁻¹ with blade tips 0.60 m from the axis. Calculate its angular velocity and the tip speed.
scheme: = 13 m s⁻¹
parts.answer: 210 rev min⁻¹ = 210×2π/60 = 22 rad s⁻¹. The tip speed is v = ωr = 22×0.60 ≈ 13 m s⁻¹.

parts.move: reject degrees in the v = ωr relation
parts.prompt: A student calculates v = ωr with ω = 90 (meaning 90 degrees per second) and r = 2.0 m, giving 180 m s⁻¹. Identify the error and give the correct speed.
scheme: ω must be in radians per second in v = ωr
parts.answer: The equation v = ωr requires ω in rad s⁻¹, not degrees per second. Converting: 90° s⁻¹ = 1.57 rad s⁻¹, so v = 1.57×2.0 = 3.1 m s⁻¹ — not 180 m s⁻¹.

parts.move: reject treating the radian as a physically separate unit in derived quantities
parts.prompt: A student notes that the unit of v/r simplifies to s⁻¹ and claims that any numerical angular speed, including one in degrees per second, can therefore be used in v = ωr. Explain the error using the definition of a radian.
scheme: Angle in radians is arc length divided by radius, a dimensionless ratio
Differentiating arc length = rθ gives v = rω for θ in radians; degree values require conversion by π/180
parts.answer: An angle in radians is the dimensionless ratio of arc length to radius. For a fixed radius, differentiating s = rθ gives v = rω with θ in radians. Although rad s⁻¹ has dimensions s⁻¹, a numerical value in degrees per second must first be multiplied by π/180.

parts.move: transfer angular-to-linear conversion to data read speed at different radii
parts.prompt: A hard drive platter rotates at 7200 rev min⁻¹. Data at radius 0.030 m passes the read head. Express the angular velocity in rad s⁻¹ and find the linear speed of the track under the head.
parts.answer: 7200 rev min⁻¹ is 7200×2π/60 = 754 rad s⁻¹. The track at r = 0.030 m sweeps past at v = 754×0.030 ≈ 23 m s⁻¹.

parts.move: translate a forward cycling speed into wheel angular velocity
parts.prompt: A bicycle travels at 6.0 m s⁻¹ on a straight road. Its wheels have diameter 0.70 m and roll without slipping. Find the wheel's angular velocity and the number of revolutions per second.
scheme: Rolling without slip: v = ωr with r = 0.35 m
Revs per second = ω/2π = 17.1/6.28 = 2.7 rev s⁻¹
parts.answer: Rolling without slipping means the contact point is instantaneously at rest, so v = ωr. With r = 0.35 m, ω = 6.0/0.35 = 17 rad s⁻¹, which is 17/2π ≈ 2.7 revolutions each second.

parts.move: combine Earth's angular velocity with radius to find surface speed and pole-star geometry
parts.prompt: Earth rotates once in 86164 s (a sidereal day). Its equatorial radius is 6.38×10⁶ m. Calculate Earth's angular velocity and the linear speed of a point on the equator.
parts.answer: One turn per 86164 s gives ω = 2π/86164 = 7.29×10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹. A point on the equator moves at v = ωr = 7.29×10⁻⁵×6.38×10⁶ ≈ 465 m s⁻¹ — fast, yet the centripetal need is tiny compared with gravity.

parts.move: combine angular velocity matching with orbital radius to reason about geostationary orbit
parts.prompt: A geostationary satellite must remain above the same point on Earth's equator. State the satellite's required angular velocity in terms of Earth's rotation, and calculate the period that ω implies. (T_Earth = 86164 s)
scheme: The satellite must match Earth's angular velocity: ω_sat = ω_Earth = 2π/86164
Its period equals Earth's sidereal day
T = 2π/ω = 86164 s ≈ 23 h 56 min, not 24 h exactly
parts.answer: Hovering over one equatorial point demands the same angular velocity as Earth: ω = 2π/86164 = 7.29×10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹. The orbital period is therefore the sidereal day, 86164 s ≈ 23 h 56 min — four minutes short of the solar 24 h, because Earth also moves around the Sun.
